claims.text: High configurational entropy can maintain the single-phase stability of equiatomic multimetal nanoparticles.
Thermally activated diffusion promotes elemental segregation in these nanoparticles.
At temperatures approaching 1923 K, thermal energy becomes sufficient to activate segregation-producing diffusion.
Surface and grain-boundary diffusion paths are especially important for segregation.
Atomic-size mismatch modulates diffusion along surfaces and grain boundaries.
Differences in elemental surface energy modulate diffusion along surfaces and grain boundaries.
Preferential atomic migration produces elemental segregation.
Continued segregation eventually produces phase separation.
Segregation and phase separation degrade catalytic performance.
Segregation and phase separation degrade thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles maintained below the critical temperature will retain a homogeneous single-phase structure relative to the as-synthesized baseline.
Nanoparticles maintained below the critical temperature will retain baseline catalytic and thermoelectric performance.
Exposure or cycling near 1900–1923 K will produce detectable elemental segregation or phase separation.
High-temperature exposure may produce distinct compositional domains or core–shell structures.
Exposure near 1900–1923 K will cause a measurable reduction in catalytic and thermoelectric efficiency.
Reactive atmospheric species such as oxygen may change the predicted stability behavior.
Large changes in nanoparticle size may alter diffusion dynamics through changes in surface-to-volume ratio.
The controlled comparison consists of equiatomic high-entropy nanoparticles treated incrementally from 473 K to 1923 K under an inert or controlled atmosphere.
Structural and chemical changes will be measured using XRD, TEM, and EDS, while performance will be assessed using catalytic and thermoelectric measurements.

The hypothesis is falsified if treatment near or above 1900 K causes neither detectable segregation or phase separation nor degradation of catalytic or thermoelectric performance relative to baseline.
